extracted.intended_audience: literate general public, aspiring poets, critics, and theatre practitioners (early-18th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical norms for producing sublime poetry, vivid descriptive passages, and appropriate theatrical epilogues; also cultural advice on comportment and modesty as represented in essays. Focuses on imitation, imagery, tone, and suitability to audience and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of celebrated authors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Critick ... proposes that he should imitate the most celebrated Authors who have gone before him, and been engaged in Works of the same nature; as in particular, that if he writes on a poetical Subject, he should consider how Homer would have spoken on such an Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation lets one great genius 'catch the Flame' from another and write 'in his Spirit, without copying servilely after him.' Example: Milton raised and ennobled his conceptions by such imitation of Longinus/Homer. Do not copy servilely; borrow spirit and grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence of ideas and management of emotion for the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Works in the sublime way should abound with magnificent Ideas and great Emotion; different parts can represent Greatness differently (e.g., 'Sixth Book... Greatness in Confusion; the seventh Affects the Imagination like the Ocean in a Calm').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether to produce tumult/agitation or a composed elevation; match imagery and pacing to the intended emotional effect (tumultuous vs calm sublimity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt high strains to audience's imaginative pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton has shewn his Judgment ... in duly qualifying those high Strains of Eastern Poetry, which were suited to Readers whose Imaginations were set to an higher pitch than those of colder Climates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using elevated/scriptural/Eastern poetic material, temper and qualify it according to the reader's cultural/psychological expectations so it resonates without alienating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scriptural and classical allusion in sacred subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many glorious strokes of Poetry upon this Subject in Holy Writ, the Author has numberless Allusions to them ... the great Critick ... has taken notice of the sublime Manner in which the Lawgiver of the Jews has describ'd the Creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For religious or cosmological themes, echo and adapt noble scriptural images (e.g., 'Let there be Light') and classical exemplars to lend majesty; select only those allusions 'proper for his Poem.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Cloathing abstract ideas in allegory and sensible images
rubrics_metrics.description: As Poetry delights in cloathing abstracted Ideas in Allegories and sensible Images, we find a magnificent Description of the Creation form'd after the same manner ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render abstract theological or cosmological concepts via vivid, tangible images (e.g., Golden Compasses, Chariots, Gates of Heaven) so readers can perceive and feel the idea; draw on Homeric and prophetic examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand, memorable incidents and instruments (use of noble conceits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Thought of the Golden Compasses is conceived altogether in Homers Spirit, and is a very noble Incident in this wonderful Description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce striking, imaginative conceits (instruments, chariots, balances, lines) that concretize cosmic actions; such noble incidents give a poetic description force and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concision with particularity in epic episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: One would wonder how the Poet could be so concise in his Description of the six Days Works, as to comprehend them within the bounds of an Episode, and at the same time so particular, as to give us a lively Idea of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to compress large events into a brief episode while selecting a few vivid particulars that make the scene feel present to the reader; balance economy with rich detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epilogue as a distinct, potentially merry performance
rubrics_metrics.description: On the British Stage they are distinct Performances by themselves, Pieces entirely detached from the Play, and no way essential to it ... the Epilogue is not unnatural because it is gay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the epilogue as its own piece — it may be comic or gay even after a serious play; historical precedent (Dryden, French 'petite piece') supports merry epilogues that send the audience away pleased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epilogue should rise from the occurrences of the play
rubrics_metrics.description: As the new Epilogue is written conformable to the Practice of our best Poets, so it is not such an one which ... might serve for any other Play; but wholly rises out of the Occurrences of the Piece it was composed for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generic, detachable epilogues: tailor the epilogue's content to the specific incidents and tone of the play so it feels organically connected rather than a stock afterpiece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and placement of comic material relative to tragic passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragi-Comedy ... breaks the Tide of the Passions while they are yet flowing; but this is nothing at all to the present Case, where they have already had their full Course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert comic relief prematurely in a tragedy (which ruins the emotional arc); comic or light pieces are permissible after the passions have run their course and the audience has had the full tragic experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and topicality of theatrical wit (avoid generic jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Epilogue ... wholly rises out of the Occurrences of the Piece it was composed for ... not such an one which ... might serve for any other Play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local, topical, or play-specific references in epilogues and prologues rather than stock jokes that could be pasted onto any performance; specificity increases perceived wit and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviour of great persons: modesty in greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the highest Instance of a noble Mind, to bear great Qualities without discovering in a Man's Behaviour any Consciousness that he is superior to the rest of the World ... He ought to think no Man valuable but for his publick Spirit, Justice and Integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent heroic or great characters (in life or fiction) as modestly bearing their gifts, showing they value their talents insofar as they serve the public good; affectation converts admiration into contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of physical presence and comportment to indicate greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prince is of that Stature which makes a Man most easily become all Parts of Exercise ... his Aspect is erect and compos'd; his Eye lively and thoughtful ... his Behaviour in an Assembly peculiarly graceful in a certain Art of mixing insensibly with the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing illustrious figures, emphasize composed bodily carriage, grace, measured action, and signs of inward steadiness rather than flashy ostentation; such traits suggest true greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female character centered on domestic duties and modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The utmost of a Woman's Character is contained in Domestick Life; she is blameable or praiseworthy according as her Carriage affects the House of her Father or her Husband ... All these may be well performed, tho a Lady should not be the very finest Woman at an Opera or an Assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise female characters (or women in social commentary) to prioritize duties as daughter, sister, wife, and mother; modest dress, moderate wit, and domestic focus are presented as durable grounds for esteem and avoid the folly of seeking public fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of ostentation in dress and entertainments
rubrics_metrics.description: He did not proportion his Provision for her to the Circumstances of her Fortune ... he admonish'd her ... that it was an Ostentation he could not but be guilty of to a Woman he had so much Pleasure in ... she must consider it as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a patron or husband provides luxuries, recipients should view them as favors or ostentation rather than intrinsic value; behavior and demeanour should not amplify vanity—avoid squandering or building a life of public display.
